newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-US shows China how to make pig's dinner.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-US shows China how to make pig's dinner.

text.p: Why is an American pulling on galoshes and sweatpants and jumping into the sludge of a Chinese pig farm to inspect swine? Because the United States is trying to prove to China that its beans are best.
China's government wants to double hog production to about one pig per person per year.

The United States, with an eye to the biggest potential feed market in the world, wants to persuade China that high protein U.S. meal, though more expensive, can fatten pigs more efficiently than Indian or South American meal which, market sources say, are high in protein but variable in quality.
Depending on global meal supply and demand and freight costs, U.S. high-protein meal can be at least $20 per tonne higher than Indian or South American meal, grains traders in Hong Kong say.
While China gobbles up normal U.S. soybean meal if the price is right, importers have largely ignored U.S. high-protein meal.
That's why Oklahoma-born livestock expert Don Bushman is spending his winter wading through the muck on various pig farms in China, overseeing feeding trials on pigs and poultry.

"China this year will import at least a million tonnes of soybean, most of which is for processing into feed, and I heard a figure as high as two million tonnes for soybean meal," said Bushman, technical director of livestock for the American Soybean Association (ASA).
"That's a lot of money China is spending on imports."

The feed trials are paid for by U.S. soybean farmers and partly funded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. U.S soybean processors, keen to see how they rank against the competition, will help pay for some of the chemical analysis.

The trials are being run with the cooperation of Chinese pig and poultry producers, and will test U.S. high protein soybean meal, Chinese high protein soybean meal, regular soybean meal from China, and soybean meal from India and South America. The aim of the feed trials is to show that consistently high-quality soybean meal, with a minimum of 47.5 percent crude protein, may cost more but is easily absorbed by hogs and fowl, producing more efficient growth and lower costs in the long run.
"We hope to show that if China does have to import, that based on quality, U.S. soybean or meal is more economical," Bushman said during a recent Hong Kong visit.
"If we can really show the economics on this, (U.S. market share) could jump to 25 percent and then grow, compared to the current five to 10 percent," he said.
India and South America split the rest of the market roughly in half between them, he said.

"A five percent improvement in feed efficiency, means you would save about 15 kg (33 lb) of feed per pig produced, or 30 yuan ($3.6) per pig," Bushman said, noting that swine producers reported current profits of around 100 yuan ($12) per pig.
As individual incomes increase, China is consuming more pork, chicken and eggs than ever before.

"Basically we're looking at a 10-11 percent increase per annum and that will continue, as long as the economy continues to grow," Bushman says, estimating that hog slaughter will jump to 500 million heads in 1996, from about 460 million last year.

Customs import figures between January and October this year show 690,000 tonnes for soybeans and 1.2 million tonnes for soymeal, an increase of 363 percent and 12,019 percent respectively over the same period last year. ($1=8.3 yuan)
